sources.title: Annie Smith Peck (Q539464), verified live via the Wikidata API (2026-11-01): label 'Annie Smith Peck', description 'American mountain climber and professor (1850-1935)', born 1850-10-19, died 1935-07-18, Korean label 애니 펙. Orientation only; not used as support for any row.

Sallie Greenwood (mountaineering historian), 'Annie Smith Peck (1850-1935)', profile in the collections of the American Alpine Club Library (2018; read in full, about 500 words). CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: the Matterhorn in 1895 and the lecture circuit that made her the public face of American mountaineering and, in the author's words, the first professional; the 1897 Mexican volcano climbs sponsored by the New York World and her claim to the highest ascent by a woman; five trips to Bolivia and Peru between 1903 and 1911 in search of the 'apex of America', often cash-strapped and relying on local men without climbing experience; the 1908 ascent of the north peak of Huascaran with Swiss guides and her optimistic height estimate of 24,000 to 26,000 feet, undone by Fanny Bullock Workman's survey; a self-supporting career as academic, lecturer, writer and photographer and then nearly two decades as a published authority and advocate for commercial opportunities in South America.

'Annie Smith Peck', Encyclopedia of World Biography (Gale; read at Encyclopedia.com, about 2,000 words). Reference biography citing her New York Times obituaries and Mazel's 'Mountaineering Women': education at Michigan and Athens, teaching posts, the shift from archaeology lectures to mountaineering lectures, the sponsored 1897 Orizaba climb, the Illampu attempts of 1903 and 1904, the Huascaran attempts of 1904, 1906 and the 1908 summit with two Swiss guides, the lost insulated suit, the dangerous descent, the 1911 memoir, later South American travel books and aerial trip. It contains some internal date slips (for example a Smith College start date), so only facts consistent with other sources are used.

'Annie Smith Peck: Record-Breaking Mountaineer', Unladylike2020 short, American Masters, PBS (10 June 2020; page and full transcript read, about 1,500 words). Documentary short featuring her biographer Hannah Kimberley and the mountaineer Vanessa O'Brien: the Matterhorn in trousers, the lecture-funded 'save up, go explore, spend every last dime' method, improvised footwear for Huascaran, the 1908 ascent, Workman's survey and the loss of the altitude record, and advertising work for a sewing-machine company. Admiring in tone; its biographer and interviewees are sympathetic.

'Legends Series: Annie Smith Peck', Explorersweb (4 July 2021; read in full, about 1,100 words). Mountaineering news site profile: the Matterhorn and clothing controversy, founding membership of the American Alpine Club in 1902, the Illampu and Huascaran climbs, the dispute with Workman over the height record and the 600 metre correction, four books, the 1929 air tour of South America and a last climb at 82. Some superlatives in it (for example a claim about first ascents by women) were not used because it gives no source.

American Alpine Club Library, Women's History Collection, items on the Huascaran height dispute (items 14, 20, 21, 99, 102 and the Annie Peck exhibit page; descriptions and transcribed text read): the club's January 1909 resolution for a committee to find the mountain's height, Workman's December 1909 cable reporting a triangulation of the north peak at 21,812 feet, Peck's handwritten reply to the club secretary of 28 December 1909, and press clippings of 1909 and 1910 on the dispute. Includes the counter-voice of her rival and Peck's own letter.

Brooklyn College Library, finding aid for the papers of Annie Smith Peck (CUNY Academic Works; read in full, about 400 words). Archival biographical note: schooling, Michigan degrees in 1878 and 1881, the Athens school, a Smith College post that she kept until 1892, then support through the lecture circuit, the 1895 Matterhorn, the 1908 Huascaran north peak and her last ascent of Mount Madison at 82. Dates for the Coropuna climb differ from other sources and are not used.

Rhode Island Historical Society, 'Miss Peck: The 19th Century Indiana Jones' (guest post by an intern, 21 July 2014; read in full, about 450 words). Local-history note on her Providence schooling, refused entry to Brown, Michigan master's degree, first woman at the Athens classical school, lectures, costume controversy and burial in Providence. Derived from the biographer's website; used only for orientation facts that other sources also give.

Wikipedia, 'Annie Smith Peck' (read; orientation only, never counted as a source and not used as support for any row). It was read to cross-check dates (Huascaran 1908, American Alpine Club 1902, Mount Madison at 82) and the Workman correction.

persistence.rationale: [src_peck_gale, src_peck_aac, src_peck_pbs, src_peck_ewb | 1903-1911 | reference biography + institutional profile + documentary + press] Gale lists Illampu attempts in 1903 and 1904 and Huascaran attempts in 1904 and 1906 before the 1908 summit, financed by magazine advances because editors liked her stories; the American Alpine Club profile says she made five trips to Bolivia and Peru between 1903 and 1911 searching for the highest peak; PBS and Explorersweb count five failed attempts or a sixth attempt (the counts differ by source but all describe repeated returns to the same mountain). The behaviour is well documented across independent summaries; the sources are mostly admiring and the exact number of attempts is inconsistent. RUBRIC_CORRECTION (lead review, before eligibility): persistence lowered from 76 / 0.62 to 74 / 0.58 because the repeated attempts are documented, but the supporting sources are largely institutional or admiring profiles and the counts of attempts differ between them.

competitiveness.rationale: [src_peck_aac, src_peck_gale, src_peck_aacdoc, src_peck_pbs | 1897-1910 | institutional profile + reference biography + archive + documentary] The American Alpine Club profile says she set out to beat the world altitude record held since 1883 and quotes her as saying that work that does not compare with men's is of little value; Gale links a lifelong urge to match her brothers to her record-seeking and says she picked Orizaba to set a women's altitude record; the club's archive shows the public contest with Fanny Bullock Workman, whose survey of the north peak at 21,812 feet ended the claim to a new record. The rivalry was largely driven by Workman and the 'brothers' explanation is the biographer's interpretation. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): reviewed as a top-risk row; lowered from 72 / 0.58 to 68 / 0.54 because the competitive motive is partly interpretive (a childhood-origin explanation in a single reference biography) and part of the rivalry evidence reflects Workman's initiative rather than Peck's own conduct.

opportunity_sensing.rationale: [src_peck_aac, src_peck_gale, src_peck_pbs, src_peck_bklyn | 1892-1930s | institutional profile + reference biography + documentary + archive finding aid] The club profile says that by 1897 she needed a new marketable feat and chose the Mexican volcanoes with New York World backing, and that she later became an expert and advocate on South American commercial opportunities; Gale says she found mountaineering talks drew audiences that archaeology lectures did not; the finding aid says she left teaching to support herself on the lecture circuit; PBS says she featured in advertising for a sewing-machine company in 1910. The market-minded reading of her choices comes from historians' interpretation rather than her own planning documents.

resourcefulness.rationale: [src_peck_aac, src_peck_gale, src_peck_pbs | 1897-1911 | institutional profile + reference biography + documentary] The club profile says she was usually cash-strapped and relied on local men without climbing experience as companions and porters, yet funded repeated expeditions as a lecturer, writer and photographer; Gale says she financed a second Huascaran attempt with a $600 magazine advance, carried a suit given to her by a museum and learned to use a hypsometer; PBS says she wore boots four sizes too large with hammered-in nails for ice traction. Improvised funding and kit are documented; the sources do not independently test how effective each improvisation was.

autonomy_need.rationale: [src_peck_bklyn, src_peck_aac, src_peck_pbs, src_peck_rihs | 1870s-1910s | archive finding aid + institutional profile + documentary + local history] After Brown refused her, she studied at Michigan; the finding aid says that after a Smith College post she decided in 1892 to support herself on the lecture circuit, and the club profile praises her ability to support herself as academic, lecturer, writer and photographer and describes her leading her own climbs; PBS reads from her writing that she meant to earn her living like any man. The self-supporting path is documented; the quoted motive is her own retrospective statement and the finding aid's dates for her teaching posts differ slightly from other sources.

risk_tolerance.rationale: [src_peck_gale, src_peck_pbs, src_peck_ewb | 1895-1908 | reference biography + documentary + press] Gale says most of her ascents were made without oxygen, that the party narrowly avoided an avalanche on the 1904 Huascaran attempt, and that the 1908 descent in the dark nearly cost them their lives (a guide later lost part of his hand and foot to frostbite); PBS and Explorersweb say she climbed the Matterhorn in trousers when women were being arrested for wearing them. She climbed with experienced guides and planned expeditions, which limits how far this shows risk-taking beyond ordinary mountaineering, and the vivid details trace to her own memoir through Gale.

conflict_tolerance.rationale: [src_peck_aacdoc, src_peck_pbs, src_peck_ewb | 1895-1910 | archive + documentary + press] The club's archive holds her 28 December 1909 letter to the club secretary answering Workman's cabled survey: she objected that the club's resolution had been passed before hearing from her and that she had been ignored by its committee, and press clippings from 1909 and 1910 record the public dispute; Explorersweb says the public arguments were harder for her than the climb, and PBS and Explorersweb record the ridicule over her trousers. She stayed public and kept lecturing through the controversy, but her own letter is the only direct statement and it is defensive in tone, so the row is moderate and dual-edged.

cross_domain_range.rationale: [src_peck_aac, src_peck_gale, src_peck_bklyn, src_peck_ewb | 1881-1932 | institutional profile + reference biography + archive + press] Michigan degrees in Greek and classical languages and a post in the first American school of classical studies at Athens, lectures on archaeology, high-altitude climbing, photography and mountaineering lectures, then four books including a commercial guide to South America and an air-travel account (Gale, the finding aid and Explorersweb list these), and the club profile calls her an expert and published authority on South American trade. The range is broad and documented, but no source evaluates her scholarship or trade writing independently.

portrait.source: Studio portrait photograph of Annie S. Peck in mountaineering dress with an ice axe and rope, credited 'Chickering Photo' (the Boston studio of Elmer Chickering, 1857-1915, whose studio continued after his death), as distributed by the New York Herald Syndicate and date-stamped 24 May 1911 on the print; Library of Congress Prints and Photographs Division, New York World-Telegram and the Sun Newspaper Photograph Collection, item 97504565, digital id cph.3c18273, call number NYWTS - BIOG--Peck, Annie S., Miss. The photograph itself is undated (it existed by 24 May 1911; its sitting date is not recorded) and the sitter is identified by the typed caption on the print. Rights review: the live Library of Congress record gives the creator credit, the 1911 date and 'No known restrictions on publication' and carries no conflicting copyright notice; that statement alone is not the basis. The basis is age: a photograph credited to a commercial studio and issued to newspapers by a press syndicate in the United States by May 1911 was published well before 1931 and its US copyright has expired. Caveats: the individual photographer within the studio and a first-publication record were not found, and the date rests on the syndicate stamp. Cropped from the library's 3289 x 4096 pixel master scan to remove the mount, stamps and caption, then downscaled to 849 x 1200 (never upscaled).
portrait.attribution: Chickering Photo, distributed by the New York Herald Syndicate, 1911; Library of Congress, New York World-Telegram and the Sun Newspaper Photograph Collection
portrait.creator: Chickering Photo (Boston studio)
